an7.66:1.1: The sun is long associated with the number seven. It is conveyed by seven golden horses (Rig Veda 4.13.03, 5.45.9; Arthavaveda 13.2.23; Maitrāyaṇī Saṁhitā 4.12.4), and has seven rays (Rig Veda 8.72.16). The seven quarters each have their own sun (Rig Veda 9.114.3), thus seven suns are mentioned (Arthavaveda 13.3.10). See also next note. If the numerological significance of the number seven is derived from the seven visible “planets”, one wonders what might happen if each caught fire.
an7.66:3.1: Sineru, also known as Neru ([ja379:3.1]()), Meru ([dn32:7.2]()), or Sumeru ([thi-ap17:53.2]()), is the *axis mundi*, the mountain around which the world revolves. The oldest reference is perhaps Taittiriya Āraṇyaka 1.7.1.3. There, Kaśyapa, the eighth above the seven Sūryas, dwells constantly on Meru, never leaving, while the other Suns illuminate different regions. Sages have gone as far as the regions around, but none reached the mountain itself. This myth, while not mentioned in the Buddhist texts, is another example of the connection between Sineru and the seven suns.
an7.66:6.2: The “seven great lakes” became a staple of later Buddhist literature, apparently from this passage, but we don’t hear of them in non-Buddhist literature.
an7.66:6.3: Anotatta (“unheated”) is mentioned as a mystical lake at [thag6.10:2.2](), while at [mil6.3.2:11.1]() it is said to be the source of the Ganges. The Buddha once ate his meal there ([pli-tv-kd1:19.2.1]()). | Moggallāna once procured some medicinal lotus for Sāriputta at the Mandākinī (“slow wanderer”) with the help of a mystical elephant ([pli-tv-kd6:20.1.8]()). A river of the same name in the Sanskrit literature is sometimes said to be the “heavenly Ganges” or the milky way.
